# solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/

## Expand description

Basic low-level memory operations.

Within the SBF environment, these are implemented as syscalls and executed by the runtime in native code.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [stubs](https://docs.rs/stubs/index.html)- Neither - `target_os=solana`nor BPF

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memcmp.html)- memcmp - ⚠
- Like C `memcmp`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memcpy.html)- memcpy - ⚠
- Like C `memcpy`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memmove.html)- memmove - ⚠
- Like C `memmove`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memset.html)- memset - ⚠
- Like C `memset`.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# camel_component_surrealdb - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/camel-component-surrealdb/0.22.0/camel_component_surrealdb/

## Expand description

camel-component-surrealdb — SurrealDB multi-model database component for rust-camel.

Provides document, graph, and vector operations through the surrealdb crate. Integrates with the datasource domain via PoolFactory.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use bundle::`- [SurrealDbBundle](https://docs.rs/bundle/struct.SurrealDbBundle.html);
- `pub use config::`- [SurrealDbEndpointConfig](https://docs.rs/config/struct.SurrealDbEndpointConfig.html);
- `pub use config::`- [SurrealDbOperation](https://docs.rs/config/enum.SurrealDbOperation.html);
- `pub use config::`- [VectorMetric](https://docs.rs/config/enum.VectorMetric.html);
- `pub use error::`- [SurrealDbError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.SurrealDbError.html);
- `pub use pool_factory::`- [redact_db_url](https://docs.rs/pool_factory/fn.redact_db_url.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bundle](https://docs.rs/bundle/index.html)
- SurrealDbBundle — groups SurrealDB component schemes and shared config.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Endpoint configuration types and URI parser for the SurrealDB component.
- [consumer](https://docs.rs/consumer/index.html)
- SurrealDbConsumer — LIVE SELECT push-based consumer.
- [endpoint](https://docs.rs/endpoint/index.html)
- SurrealDbEndpoint — creates producers, consumers, and polling consumers.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for the SurrealDB component.
- [headers](https://docs.rs/headers/index.html)
- Header constant definitions for the SurrealDB component.
- [polling](https://docs.rs/polling/index.html)
- SurrealDbPollingConsumer — PollingConsumer for pollEnrich and camel_poll support.
- [pool_](https://docs.rs/pool_factory/index.html)- factory
- SurrealDB PoolFactory — creates Surrealclients and registers with the datasource catalog.
- [producer](https://docs.rs/producer/index.html)
- SurrealDbProducer — Serviceimplementation handling 8 producer operations.
- [query](https://docs.rs/query/index.html)
- Identifier validation and SurrealQL query builders for operations that have no SDK fluent equivalent.
- [vector](https://docs.rs/vector/index.html)
- Vector helpers for extracting `Vec<f32>`from SurrealDB JSON values.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Surreal](https://docs.rs/struct.SurrealDbComponent.html)- DbComponent
- SurrealDB component — factory for `surrealdb:`endpoints.

# autoconf_rs_cli - Rust

## Expand description

autoconf-rs-cli shared library.

Provides the CLI argument parsing harness used by all 8 Autoconf binaries. Each binary is a thin wrapper that delegates to autoconf-rs-core.

# mermaid_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mermaid-runtime/0.15.1/mermaid_runtime/

## Expand description

Daemon-safe runtime services.

The TUI reducer remains the correctness core, but durable concerns that a daemon or future remote client will also need live here. The first slice is SQLite-backed state for tasks, approvals, processes, and the future provider/memory/checkpoint tables.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Open](https://docs.rs/enum.OpenIntent.html)- Intent
- What kind of access an `open_beneath`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [create_](https://docs.rs/fn.create_dir_all_beneath.html)- dir_ - all_ - beneath
- Confined `mkdir -p`for a`root`-relative directory path: creates each missing component beneath`root`, refusing to descend through a symlink that escapes (#77). On Linux:`mkdirat`+`openat2(RESOLVE_BENEATH)`per component; otherwise the`contain_within_canonical`+`std::fs`fallback.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_beneath.html)- beneath
- Open `root`-relative`rel`for`intent`**without ever traversing out of**— closing the check-then-write TOCTOU where an intermediate directory is swapped for a symlink after a lexical path check but before the operation (#77). The returned`root``File`
- [remove_](https://docs.rs/fn.remove_file_beneath.html)- file_ - beneath
- Confined unlink of a `root`-relative file (#77): opens the parent under`RESOLVE_BENEATH`and`unlinkat`s the leaf, so a swapped-in symlink parent can’t redirect the delete outside`root`.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_atomic_beneath.html)- atomic_ - beneath
- Atomically write `bytes`to`root`-relative`rel`without ever traversing out of`root`. The temp file is created and`renameat`-swapped beneath the*same*confined directory fd as the destination (Linux`openat2(RESOLVE_BENEATH)`), so a parent dir swapped for an escaping symlink after a path check can’t redirect the write (#77), AND a crash/kill/disk-full mid-write leaves the previous file intact instead of a truncated one —`open_beneath`+`WriteTruncate`gives the first guarantee but not the second. Falls back to`contain_within_canonical`+ by-path`crate::write_atomic``openat2`kernels (the same best-effort posture as the other helpers).

# cu_feetech - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu-feetech/1.0.0/cu_feetech/

## Expand description

Feetech STS/SCS serial bus servo bridge for Copper.

This crate provides a [ CuBridge](https://docs.rs/cu29-runtime/1.0.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/cu29_runtime/cubridge/trait.CuBridge.html) that communicates with Feetech STS/SCS
serial bus servos (such as the

**STS3215**used in SO-100 / SO-101 robot arms) over a half-duplex serial (UART) bus.

[§](https://docs.rs#protocol-overview)Protocol overview

Feetech servos use a Dynamixel-style packet protocol:

```
TX:  [0xFF 0xFF] [ID] [LENGTH] [INSTRUCTION] [PARAM …] [CHECKSUM]
RX:  [0xFF 0xFF] [ID] [LENGTH] [ERROR]       [DATA …]  [CHECKSUM]
```
The bus is half-duplex: after each instruction packet the master reads back a status packet (except for broadcast sync-write, which has no response).

[§](https://docs.rs#channels)Channels

| Direction | Channel id | Payload | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rx | `positions` | `JointPositions` | Present positions read from servos |
| Tx | `goal_positions` | `JointPositions` | Goal positions written to servos |

[§](https://docs.rs#position-values)Position values

The unit of published / consumed positions depends on the `"units"` config
key:

| Value | Meaning | Calibration required? |
|---|---|---|
| `"raw"` | Raw 16-bit register values (0..65535). Default. | No |
| `"deg"` | Degrees relative to calibration center. | Yes |
| `"rad"` | Radians relative to calibration center. | Yes |
| `"normalize"` | [-1, 1] over calibrated min..max (same scale for leader/follower). | Yes |

When using `"deg"`, `"rad"`, or `"normalize"`, set `"calibration_file"` to the path of a
JSON file generated by the `feetech-calibrate` tool.  The center (zero) of
each servo is the midpoint of its calibrated min/max range.  Optionally
set `"ticks_per_rev"` (raw units per 360°); the value is model-dependent
(default 4096, e.g. for STS3215).

[§](https://docs.rs#torque-behaviour)Torque behaviour

- When **Tx writers are connected**(commander mode) the bridge enables torque on`start`
- When **no Tx writers are connected**(follower / teach mode) torque is left**disabled**so the arm can be moved freely by hand while positions are read back.
- On `stop`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [calibration](https://docs.rs/calibration/index.html)
- Calibration data and unit conversions for Feetech servos.
- [messages](https://docs.rs/messages/index.html)
- Message types for the Feetech bridge.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Feetech](https://docs.rs/struct.FeetechBridge.html)- Bridge
- Bidirectional bridge for Feetech STS/SCS serial bus servos.
- [Resources](https://docs.rs/struct.Resources.html)
- [RxChannels](https://docs.rs/struct.RxChannels.html)
- [TxChannels](https://docs.rs/struct.TxChannels.html)

---

# cumulus_client_consensus_relay_chain - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cumulus-client-consensus-relay-chain/0.32.0/cumulus_client_consensus_relay_chain/

## Expand description

The relay-chain provided consensus algorithm for parachains.

This is the simplest consensus algorithm you can use when developing a parachain. It is a permission-less consensus algorithm that doesn’t require any staking or similar to join as a collator. In this algorithm the consensus is provided by the relay-chain. This works in the following way.

-
Each node that sees itself as a collator is free to build a parachain candidate.
-
This parachain candidate is send to the parachain validators that are part of the relay chain.
-
The parachain validators validate at most X different parachain candidates, where X is the total number of parachain validators.
-
The parachain candidate that is backed by the most validators is chosen by the relay-chain block producer to be added as backed candidate on chain.
-
After the parachain candidate got backed and included, all collators start at 1.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Verifier](https://docs.rs/struct.Verifier.html)
- A verifier that just checks the inherents.

---

# sim_lib_midi_shapes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-midi-shapes/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_midi_shapes/

## Expand description

Shape and citizen surfaces that expose the MIDI model to the SIM runtime.

This crate bridges the [ sim_lib_midi_core](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-midi-core/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_midi_core/index.html)/

[data types into two SIM facilities:](https://docs.rs/sim-lib-midi-smf/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_lib_midi_smf/index.html)

`sim_lib_midi_smf`- A string codec (the `encode_*`/`decode_*`functions) that round-trips MIDI events, channel messages, meta events, SysEx, raw bytes, tracks, and SMF files through a compact`#(...)`reader form, with errors reported as`MidiShapeError`
- Citizen descriptors (`MidiEventDescriptor``MidiChannelMessageDescriptor``MidiMetaEventDescriptor``MidiSmfTrackDescriptor``MidiSmfFileDescriptor``MidiShapesLib``midi/*`shape values.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The channel-message codec round-trips through the reader form:

```
use sim_lib_midi_shapes::{decode_channel_message, encode_channel_message};
let form = "#(Channel NoteOn 0 60 100)";
let message = decode_channel_message(form).unwrap();
assert_eq!(encode_channel_message(message), form);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiChannelMessageDescriptor.html)- Channel - Message - Descriptor
- Citizen descriptor wrapping the canonical `midi/ChannelMessage`string form.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiEventDescriptor.html)- Event - Descriptor
- Citizen descriptor wrapping the canonical `midi/MidiEvent`string form.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiMetaEventDescriptor.html)- Meta - Event - Descriptor
- Citizen descriptor wrapping the canonical `midi/MetaEvent`string form.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiShapesLib.html)- Shapes - Lib
- Host-registered lib that publishes the `midi/*`shape values (TickTime, MidiEvent, ChannelMessage, MetaEvent, SysExEvent, RawBytes, SmfTrack, SmfFile, and the I/O factory rows) into a running runtime.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiSmfFileDescriptor.html)- SmfFile - Descriptor
- Citizen descriptor wrapping the canonical `midi/SmfFile`string form.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiSmfTrackDescriptor.html)- SmfTrack - Descriptor
- Citizen descriptor wrapping the canonical `midi/SmfTrack`string form.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Midi](https://docs.rs/enum.MidiShapeError.html)- Shape - Error
- Errors raised while decoding a MIDI string shape, named by the shape that failed to parse.

# omq_tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/omq-tokio/0.15.0/omq_tokio/

## Expand description

omq-tokio - tokio-runtime backend for omq.

Wire-compatible with libzmq. All 11 standard socket types plus 7 draft types, TCP / IPC / inproc / UDP transports, NULL / CURVE / blake3zmq mechanisms, lz4+tcp compression transport.

The codec, message types, mechanism handshakes, and routing
algorithms live in the runtime-agnostic `omq-proto` crate.
This crate provides the tokio glue: per-connection drivers,
transport implementations, and the public `Socket` actor.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use socket::`- [MonitorStream](https://docs.rs/socket/monitor/struct.MonitorStream.html);
- `pub use socket::`- [Socket](https://docs.rs/socket/handle/struct.Socket.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [endpoint](https://docs.rs/endpoint/index.html)
- Endpoint parsing and formatting.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- Connection driver: tokio glue between a `Transport`’s stream and the sans-I/O ZMTP [`Connection`].
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error and Result types.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- Message, Frame, and Payload types.
- [options](https://docs.rs/options/index.html)
- Socket options: typed builder.
- [proto](https://docs.rs/proto/index.html)
- Sans-I/O ZMTP 3.x codec.
- [socket](https://docs.rs/socket/index.html)
- Socket: the public handle and its backing actor.
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- Transport abstraction and implementations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Authenticator](https://docs.rs/struct.Authenticator.html)
- Server-side admission callback shared by every encrypting
mechanism (CURVE, BLAKE3ZMQ). Invoked once per handshake after
vouch verification, before READY is sent. Returning `false`rejects the client; the handshake aborts.`Arc`-wrapped so the closure can be cloned through`MechanismSetup`.
- [Blake3](https://docs.rs/struct.Blake3ZmqKeypair.html)- ZmqKeypair
- X25519 keypair used by both client and server sides of the BLAKE3ZMQ
handshake. The 32-byte secret half is `Drop`-zeroed.
- [Blake3](https://docs.rs/struct.Blake3ZmqPublicKey.html)- ZmqPublic - Key
- [Blake3](https://docs.rs/struct.Blake3ZmqSecretKey.html)- ZmqSecret - Key
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.ConnectionStatus.html)- Status
- Live status of a connected peer, returned by `Socket::connection_info`.
- [Curve](https://docs.rs/struct.CurveCookieKeyring.html)- Cookie - Keyring
- [Curve](https://docs.rs/struct.CurveKeypair.html)- Keypair
- A long-term Curve25519 keypair.
- [Curve](https://docs.rs/struct.CurvePublicKey.html)- Public - Key
- 32-byte Curve25519 public key.
- [Curve](https://docs.rs/struct.CurveSecretKey.html)- Secret - Key
- 32-byte Curve25519 secret key. Zeroed on drop.
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.EndpointSpec.html)- Spec
- An endpoint plus an optional role prefix. Parsed from strings like
`"@tcp://*:5555"`or`">tcp://host:5555"`or just`"tcp://host:5555"`.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.Frame.html)
- A single ZMTP frame on the wire.
- [Frame](https://docs.rs/struct.FrameFlags.html)- Flags
- ZMTP frame flags.
- [Mechanism](https://docs.rs/struct.MechanismPeerInfo.html)- Peer - Info
- Information passed to an `Authenticator`
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.Message.html)
- A message: one or more parts delivered atomically over a ZMTP socket.
- [Message](https://docs.rs/struct.MessageIter.html)- Iter
- Public iterator yielding `Bytes`per message part.
- [Options](https://docs.rs/struct.Options.html)
- Per-socket configuration.
- [Part](https://docs.rs/struct.PartCountError.html)- Count - Error
- Error returned by `Message::try_as_parts`
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/struct.PeerInfo.html)- Info
- Rich context passed on per-connection events. Cheap to clone: heavy fields are reference-counted.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Disconnect](https://docs.rs/enum.DisconnectReason.html)- Reason
- Why a connection was closed.
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/enum.Endpoint.html)
- A transport endpoint.
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/enum.EndpointRole.html)- Role
- Role for an endpoint in a single-string spec: bind, connect, or default.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Every expected failure mode in omq.
- [IpcPath](https://docs.rs/enum.IpcPath.html)
- IPC path, possibly in the Linux abstract namespace (leading `@`). Only available on Unix platforms.
- [Keep](https://docs.rs/enum.KeepAlive.html)- Alive
- TCP keepalive policy. `Default`leaves the OS defaults alone (matches libzmq’s`ZMQ_TCP_KEEPALIVE = -1`);`Disabled`clears`SO_KEEPALIVE`;`Enabled`sets`SO_KEEPALIVE`and pins the three timing knobs.
- [Mechanism](https://docs.rs/enum.MechanismSetup.html)- Setup
- Security-mechanism configuration passed to [`Connection::new`] and stored in`Options``curve`feature; BLAKE3ZMQ behind`blake3zmq`.
- [Monitor](https://docs.rs/enum.MonitorEvent.html)- Event
- A connection-lifecycle event emitted by a socket.
- [Monitor](https://docs.rs/enum.MonitorRecvError.html)- Recv - Error
- [Monitor](https://docs.rs/enum.MonitorTryRecvError.html)- TryRecv - Error
- [OnMute](https://docs.rs/enum.OnMute.html)
- What to do when the send HWM is reached and a new message arrives.
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/enum.PeerCommandKind.html)- Command - Kind
- The peer-sent commands surfaced via `MonitorEvent::PeerCommand`
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/enum.PeerIdent.html)- Ident
- Opaque peer identifier returned by transport accept paths. Used in monitor events and by identity-routed strategies that want to distinguish peers before the ZMTP handshake completes.
- [Reconnect](https://docs.rs/enum.ReconnectPolicy.html)- Policy
- Reconnection policy applied after a lost connection on `connect()`sockets.
- [Socket](https://docs.rs/enum.SocketType.html)- Type
- All 19 ZMTP socket types.
- [TrySend](https://docs.rs/enum.TrySendError.html)- Error
- Error returned by `Socket::try_send`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_compatible.html)- compatible
- ZMTP socket-type compatibility matrix (RFC 23 + 37 + 48 + 52).

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Mechanism](https://docs.rs/type.MechanismConfig.html)- Config
- Backward-compatible alias. `MechanismSetup`
- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- Convenience alias with `Error`as the default error type.

# omq_zmq - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/omq-libzmq/0.4.10/omq_zmq/

## Expand description

omq-libzmq – libzmq-compatible C interface backed by omq-tokio.

[§](https://docs.rs#panic-safety)Panic safety

Since Rust 1.71, panics in `extern "C"` functions abort rather than
UB. No `catch_unwind` wrappers are used: wrapping 50+ FFI functions
in `AssertUnwindSafe` would weaken static guarantees for marginal
benefit. libzmq itself aborts on internal errors, so abort-on-panic
is acceptable behavior for a drop-in replacement.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use curve::`- [zmq_curve_keypair](https://docs.rs/curve/fn.zmq_curve_keypair.html);
- `pub use curve::`- [zmq_curve_public](https://docs.rs/curve/fn.zmq_curve_public.html);
- `pub use curve::`- [zmq_z85_decode](https://docs.rs/curve/fn.zmq_z85_decode.html);
- `pub use curve::`- [zmq_z85_encode](https://docs.rs/curve/fn.zmq_z85_encode.html);
- `pub use poll::`- [zmq_poll](https://docs.rs/poll/fn.zmq_poll.html);
- `pub use proxy::`- [zmq_proxy](https://docs.rs/proxy/fn.zmq_proxy.html);
- `pub use proxy::`- [zmq_proxy_steerable](https://docs.rs/proxy/fn.zmq_proxy_steerable.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [curve](https://docs.rs/curve/index.html)
- CURVE key utilities and Z85 encode/decode.

# cu29_helpers - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cu29-helpers/1.0.0/cu29_helpers/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cu29-helpers)cu29-helpers

This crate is intentionally retired.

It exists as a compatibility stub so downstream users who still depend on
`cu29-helpers` get a compile-time migration message that points them at the new
generated app builder API:

If the app needs a custom clock, logger, config override, or resource factory,
set those through the builder before calling `.build()`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [compatibility_](https://docs.rs/compatibility_stub/index.html)- stub
- Compatibility stub for workspace builds.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/3.1.0/src/solana_program_memory/lib.rs.html

# solana_program_memory/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![no_std]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_cfg))]
[3](https://docs.rs#3)
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! Basic low-level memory operations.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Within the SBF environment, these are implemented as syscalls and executed by
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! the runtime in native code.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)#[cfg(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))]
[12](https://docs.rs#12)pub mod syscalls {
[13](https://docs.rs#13)    pub use solana_define_syscall::definitions::{
[14](https://docs.rs#14)        sol_memcmp_, sol_memcpy_, sol_memmove_, sol_memset_,
[15](https://docs.rs#15)    };
[16](https://docs.rs#16)}
[17](https://docs.rs#17)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)/// Check that two regions do not overlap.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)#[cfg(any(test, not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))))]
[20](https://docs.rs#20)fn is_nonoverlapping(src: usize, src_len: usize, dst: usize, dst_len: usize) -> bool {
[21](https://docs.rs#21)    // If the absolute distance between the ptrs is at least as big as the size of the other,
[22](https://docs.rs#22)    // they do not overlap.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)    if src > dst {
[24](https://docs.rs#24)        src.saturating_sub(dst) >= dst_len
[25](https://docs.rs#25)    } else {
[26](https://docs.rs#26)        dst.saturating_sub(src) >= src_len
[27](https://docs.rs#27)    }
[28](https://docs.rs#28)}
[29](https://docs.rs#29)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)#[cfg(not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf")))]
[31](https://docs.rs#31)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[32](https://docs.rs#32)pub mod stubs {
[33](https://docs.rs#33)    use super::is_nonoverlapping;
[34](https://docs.rs#34)    /// # Safety
[35](https://docs.rs#35)    pub unsafe fn sol_memcpy(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, n: usize) {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)        // cannot be overlapping
[37](https://docs.rs#37)        assert!(
[38](https://docs.rs#38)            is_nonoverlapping(src as usize, n, dst as usize, n),
[39](https://docs.rs#39)            "memcpy does not support overlapping regions"
[40](https://docs.rs#40)        );
[41](https://docs.rs#41)        core::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(src, dst, n);
[42](https://docs.rs#42)    }
[43](https://docs.rs#43)    /// # Safety
[44](https://docs.rs#44)    pub unsafe fn sol_memmove(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, n: usize) {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)        core::ptr::copy(src, dst, n);
[46](https://docs.rs#46)    }
[47](https://docs.rs#47)    /// # Safety
[48](https://docs.rs#48)    pub unsafe fn sol_memcmp(s1: *const u8, s2: *const u8, n: usize, result: *mut i32) {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)        let mut i = 0;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)        while i < n {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)            let a = *s1.add(i);
[52](https://docs.rs#52)            let b = *s2.add(i);
[53](https://docs.rs#53)            if a != b {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)                *result = a as i32 - b as i32;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)                return;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)            }
[57](https://docs.rs#57)            i += 1;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)        }
[59](https://docs.rs#59)        *result = 0
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    }
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    /// # Safety
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    pub unsafe fn sol_memset(s: *mut u8, c: u8, n: usize) {
[63](https://docs.rs#63)        let s = core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(s, n);
[64](https://docs.rs#64)        for val in s.iter_mut().take(n) {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)            *val = c;
[66](https://docs.rs#66)        }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    }
[68](https://docs.rs#68)}
[69](https://docs.rs#69)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// Like C `memcpy`.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)///
[72](https://docs.rs#72)/// # Arguments
[73](https://docs.rs#73)///
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// - `dst` - Destination
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// - `src` - Source
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// - `n` - Number of bytes to copy
[77](https://docs.rs#77)///
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// # Errors
[79](https://docs.rs#79)///
[80](https://docs.rs#80)/// When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// the program will abort.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// The memory regions spanning `n` bytes from `dst` and `src` from the start
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// of `dst` and `src` must not overlap. If they do, then the program will abort
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// or, if run outside of the SBF VM, will panic.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)///
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// # Safety
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// lengths of the `dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will copy
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// bytes to and from beyond the slices.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// likely introduce undefined behavior.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)#[inline]
[97](https://docs.rs#97)pub unsafe fn sol_memcpy(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8], n: usize) {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    #[cfg(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))]
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    syscalls::sol_memcpy_(dst.as_mut_ptr(), src.as_ptr(), n as u64);
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    #[cfg(not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf")))]
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    stubs::sol_memcpy(dst.as_mut_ptr(), src.as_ptr(), n);
[103](https://docs.rs#103)}
[104](https://docs.rs#104)

[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// - `src` - Source
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// - `n` - Number of bytes to copy
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// # Errors
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
[116](https://docs.rs#116)/// from from `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program

[200](https://docs.rs#200)mod tests {
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    use super::*;
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    #[test]
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    fn test_is_nonoverlapping() {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        for dst in 0..8 {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            assert!(is_nonoverlapping(10, 3, dst, 3));
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        for dst in 8..13 {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            assert!(!is_nonoverlapping(10, 3, dst, 3));
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        }
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        for dst in 13..20 {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)            assert!(is_nonoverlapping(10, 3, dst, 3));
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        assert!(is_nonoverlapping(usize::MAX, 3, usize::MAX - 1, 1));
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        assert!(!is_nonoverlapping(usize::MAX, 2, usize::MAX - 1, 3));
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    }
[217](https://docs.rs#217)}

# sol_memcmp in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/3.1.0/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memcmp.html

## Expand description

Like C `memcmp`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `s1`- Slice to be compared
- `s2`- Slice to be compared
- `n`- Number of bytes to compare

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
the program will abort.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

It does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the lengths of the
`dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will read bytes beyond the
slices.

Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
likely introduce undefined behavior.

---

# sol_memcpy in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/3.1.0/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memcpy.html

## Expand description

Like C `memcpy`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `dst`- Destination
- `src`- Source
- `n`- Number of bytes to copy

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
the program will abort.

The memory regions spanning `n` bytes from `dst` and `src` from the start
of `dst` and `src` must not overlap. If they do, then the program will abort
or, if run outside of the SBF VM, will panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the
lengths of the `dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will copy
bytes to and from beyond the slices.

Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
likely introduce undefined behavior.

---

# sol_memmove in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/3.1.0/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memmove.html

## Expand description

Like C `memmove`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `dst`- Destination
- `src`- Source
- `n`- Number of bytes to copy

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
from from `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program
will abort.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The same safety rules apply as in [ ptr::copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ptr/fn.copy.html).

---

# sol_memset in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/3.1.0/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memset.html

## Expand description

Like C `memset`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `s`- Slice to be set
- `c`- Repeated byte to set
- `n`- Number of bytes to set

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory region spanning `n` bytes
from from the start of `s` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program
will abort.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the length
of the `s` slice passed to it — it will write bytes beyond the
slice.

Specifying an `n` greater than the length of `s` will likely introduce
undefined behavior.

# solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-memory/latest/solana_program_memory/

## Expand description

Basic low-level memory operations.

Within the SBF environment, these are implemented as syscalls and executed by the runtime in native code.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [stubs](https://docs.rs/stubs/index.html)- Neither - `target_os=solana`nor BPF

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memcmp.html)- memcmp - ⚠
- Like C `memcmp`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memcpy.html)- memcpy - ⚠
- Like C `memcpy`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memmove.html)- memmove - ⚠
- Like C `memmove`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memset.html)- memset - ⚠
- Like C `memset`.

# solana-program-memory 3.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-memory/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-memory/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_memory/index.html

## Expand description

Basic low-level memory operations.

Within the SBF environment, these are implemented as syscalls and executed by the runtime in native code.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [stubs](https://docs.rs/stubs/index.html)- Neither - `target_os=solana`nor BPF

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memcmp.html)- memcmp - ⚠
- Like C `memcmp`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memcpy.html)- memcpy - ⚠
- Like C `memcpy`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memmove.html)- memmove - ⚠
- Like C `memmove`.
- [sol_](https://docs.rs/fn.sol_memset.html)- memset - ⚠
- Like C `memset`.

---

[3](https://docs.rs#3)
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! Basic low-level memory operations.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Within the SBF environment, these are implemented as syscalls and executed by
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! the runtime in native code.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)#[cfg(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))]
[12](https://docs.rs#12)pub mod syscalls {
[13](https://docs.rs#13)    pub use solana_define_syscall::definitions::{
[14](https://docs.rs#14)        sol_memcmp_, sol_memcpy_, sol_memmove_, sol_memset_,
[15](https://docs.rs#15)    };
[16](https://docs.rs#16)}
[17](https://docs.rs#17)
[18](https://docs.rs#18)/// Check that two regions do not overlap.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)#[cfg(any(test, not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))))]
[20](https://docs.rs#20)fn is_nonoverlapping(src: usize, src_len: usize, dst: usize, dst_len: usize) -> bool {
[21](https://docs.rs#21)    // If the absolute distance between the ptrs is at least as big as the size of the other,
[22](https://docs.rs#22)    // they do not overlap.
[23](https://docs.rs#23)    if src > dst {
[24](https://docs.rs#24)        src.saturating_sub(dst) >= dst_len
[25](https://docs.rs#25)    } else {
[26](https://docs.rs#26)        dst.saturating_sub(src) >= src_len
[27](https://docs.rs#27)    }
[28](https://docs.rs#28)}
[29](https://docs.rs#29)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)#[cfg(not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf")))]
[31](https://docs.rs#31)#[allow(clippy::arithmetic_side_effects)]
[32](https://docs.rs#32)pub mod stubs {
[33](https://docs.rs#33)    use super::is_nonoverlapping;
[34](https://docs.rs#34)    /// # Safety
[35](https://docs.rs#35)    pub unsafe fn sol_memcpy(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, n: usize) {
[36](https://docs.rs#36)        // cannot be overlapping
[37](https://docs.rs#37)        assert!(
[38](https://docs.rs#38)            is_nonoverlapping(src as usize, n, dst as usize, n),
[39](https://docs.rs#39)            "memcpy does not support overlapping regions"
[40](https://docs.rs#40)        );
[41](https://docs.rs#41)        core::ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(src, dst, n);
[42](https://docs.rs#42)    }
[43](https://docs.rs#43)    /// # Safety
[44](https://docs.rs#44)    pub unsafe fn sol_memmove(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, n: usize) {
[45](https://docs.rs#45)        core::ptr::copy(src, dst, n);
[46](https://docs.rs#46)    }
[47](https://docs.rs#47)    /// # Safety
[48](https://docs.rs#48)    pub unsafe fn sol_memcmp(s1: *const u8, s2: *const u8, n: usize, result: *mut i32) {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)        let mut i = 0;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)        while i < n {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)            let a = *s1.add(i);
[52](https://docs.rs#52)            let b = *s2.add(i);
[53](https://docs.rs#53)            if a != b {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)                *result = a as i32 - b as i32;
[55](https://docs.rs#55)                return;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)            }
[57](https://docs.rs#57)            i += 1;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)        }
[59](https://docs.rs#59)        *result = 0
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    }
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    /// # Safety
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    pub unsafe fn sol_memset(s: *mut u8, c: u8, n: usize) {
[63](https://docs.rs#63)        let s = core::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(s, n);
[64](https://docs.rs#64)        for val in s.iter_mut().take(n) {
[65](https://docs.rs#65)            *val = c;
[66](https://docs.rs#66)        }
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    }
[68](https://docs.rs#68)}
[69](https://docs.rs#69)
[70](https://docs.rs#70)/// Like C `memcpy`.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)///
[72](https://docs.rs#72)/// # Arguments
[73](https://docs.rs#73)///
[74](https://docs.rs#74)/// - `dst` - Destination
[75](https://docs.rs#75)/// - `src` - Source
[76](https://docs.rs#76)/// - `n` - Number of bytes to copy
[77](https://docs.rs#77)///
[78](https://docs.rs#78)/// # Errors
[79](https://docs.rs#79)///
[80](https://docs.rs#80)/// When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
[81](https://docs.rs#81)/// from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// the program will abort.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// The memory regions spanning `n` bytes from `dst` and `src` from the start
[85](https://docs.rs#85)/// of `dst` and `src` must not overlap. If they do, then the program will abort
[86](https://docs.rs#86)/// or, if run outside of the SBF VM, will panic.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)///
[88](https://docs.rs#88)/// # Safety
[89](https://docs.rs#89)///
[90](https://docs.rs#90)/// This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// lengths of the `dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will copy
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// bytes to and from beyond the slices.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///
[94](https://docs.rs#94)/// Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// likely introduce undefined behavior.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)#[inline]
[97](https://docs.rs#97)pub unsafe fn sol_memcpy(dst: &mut [u8], src: &[u8], n: usize) {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    #[cfg(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))]
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    syscalls::sol_memcpy_(dst.as_mut_ptr(), src.as_ptr(), n as u64);
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    #[cfg(not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf")))]
[102](https://docs.rs#102)    stubs::sol_memcpy(dst.as_mut_ptr(), src.as_ptr(), n);
[103](https://docs.rs#103)}
[104](https://docs.rs#104)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)/// Like C `memmove`.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)///
[107](https://docs.rs#107)/// # Arguments
[108](https://docs.rs#108)///
[109](https://docs.rs#109)/// - `dst` - Destination
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// - `src` - Source
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// - `n` - Number of bytes to copy
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// # Errors
[114](https://docs.rs#114)///
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
[116](https://docs.rs#116)/// from from `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// will abort.
[118](https://docs.rs#118)///
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// # Safety
[120](https://docs.rs#120)///
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// The same safety rules apply as in [`ptr::copy`].
[122](https://docs.rs#122)///
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// [`ptr::copy`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ptr/fn.copy.html
[124](https://docs.rs#124)#[inline]
[125](https://docs.rs#125)pub unsafe fn sol_memmove(dst: *mut u8, src: *const u8, n: usize) {

[127](https://docs.rs#127)    syscalls::sol_memmove_(dst, src, n as u64);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)

[130](https://docs.rs#130)    stubs::sol_memmove(dst, src, n);
[131](https://docs.rs#131)}
[132](https://docs.rs#132)
[133](https://docs.rs#133)/// Like C `memcmp`.
[134](https://docs.rs#134)///
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// # Arguments
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// - `s1` - Slice to be compared
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// - `s2` - Slice to be compared
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// - `n` - Number of bytes to compare
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// # Errors
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///
[143](https://docs.rs#143)/// When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
[144](https://docs.rs#144)/// from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)/// the program will abort.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)///
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// # Safety
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// It does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the lengths of the
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// `dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will read bytes beyond the
[151](https://docs.rs#151)/// slices.
[152](https://docs.rs#152)///
[153](https://docs.rs#153)/// Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// likely introduce undefined behavior.
[155](https://docs.rs#155)#[inline]
[156](https://docs.rs#156)pub unsafe fn sol_memcmp(s1: &[u8], s2: &[u8], n: usize) -> i32 {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)    let mut result: MaybeUninit<i32> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    #[cfg(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf"))]
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    syscalls::sol_memcmp_(s1.as_ptr(), s2.as_ptr(), n as u64, result.as_mut_ptr());
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    #[cfg(not(any(target_os = "solana", target_arch = "bpf")))]
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    stubs::sol_memcmp(s1.as_ptr(), s2.as_ptr(), n, result.as_mut_ptr());
[164](https://docs.rs#164)
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    result.assume_init()
[166](https://docs.rs#166)}

[172](https://docs.rs#172)/// - `s` - Slice to be set
[173](https://docs.rs#173)/// - `c` - Repeated byte to set
[174](https://docs.rs#174)/// - `n` - Number of bytes to set
[175](https://docs.rs#175)///

[177](https://docs.rs#177)///
[178](https://docs.rs#178)/// When executed within a SBF program, the memory region spanning `n` bytes
[179](https://docs.rs#179)/// from from the start of `s` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program
[180](https://docs.rs#180)/// will abort.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)///
[182](https://docs.rs#182)/// # Safety
[183](https://docs.rs#183)///
[184](https://docs.rs#184)/// This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the length
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// of the `s` slice passed to it — it will write bytes beyond the
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// slice.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)///

[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// undefined behavior.

[193](https://docs.rs#193)    syscalls::sol_memset_(s.as_mut_ptr(), c, n as u64);

[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    #[test]
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    fn test_is_nonoverlapping() {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        for dst in 0..8 {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)            assert!(is_nonoverlapping(10, 3, dst, 3));
[207](https://docs.rs#207)        }
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        for dst in 8..13 {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)            assert!(!is_nonoverlapping(10, 3, dst, 3));
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        }
[211](https://docs.rs#211)        for dst in 13..20 {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)            assert!(is_nonoverlapping(10, 3, dst, 3));
[213](https://docs.rs#213)        }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        assert!(is_nonoverlapping(usize::MAX, 3, usize::MAX - 1, 1));
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        assert!(!is_nonoverlapping(usize::MAX, 2, usize::MAX - 1, 3));
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    }

# sol_memcmp in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-memory/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memcmp.html

## Expand description

Like C `memcmp`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `s1`- Slice to be compared
- `s2`- Slice to be compared
- `n`- Number of bytes to compare

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
the program will abort.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

It does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the lengths of the
`dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will read bytes beyond the
slices.

Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
likely introduce undefined behavior.

---

# sol_memcpy in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-memory/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memcpy.html

## Expand description

Like C `memcpy`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `dst`- Destination
- `src`- Source
- `n`- Number of bytes to copy

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
from from the start of `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not,
the program will abort.

The memory regions spanning `n` bytes from `dst` and `src` from the start
of `dst` and `src` must not overlap. If they do, then the program will abort
or, if run outside of the SBF VM, will panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the
lengths of the `dst` and `src` slices passed to it — it will copy
bytes to and from beyond the slices.

Specifying an `n` greater than either the length of `dst` or `src` will
likely introduce undefined behavior.

---

# sol_memmove in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-memory/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memmove.html

## Expand description

Like C `memmove`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `dst`- Destination
- `src`- Source
- `n`- Number of bytes to copy

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory regions spanning `n` bytes
from from `dst` and `src` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program
will abort.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The same safety rules apply as in [ ptr::copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/ptr/fn.copy.html).

---

# sol_memset in solana_program_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-memory/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_memory/fn.sol_memset.html

## Expand description

Like C `memset`.

[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `s`- Slice to be set
- `c`- Repeated byte to set
- `n`- Number of bytes to set

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

When executed within a SBF program, the memory region spanning `n` bytes
from from the start of `s` must be mapped program memory. If not, the program
will abort.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This function does not verify that `n` is less than or equal to the length
of the `s` slice passed to it — it will write bytes beyond the
slice.

Specifying an `n` greater than the length of `s` will likely introduce
undefined behavior.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

[§](https://docs.rs#related-projects)Related Projects

Augment clap:

- [wild](https://crates.io/crates/wild)for supporting wildcards (- `*`) on Windows like you do Linux
- [argfile](https://crates.io/crates/argfile)for loading additional arguments from a file (aka response files)
- [shadow-rs](https://crates.io/crates/shadow-rs)for generating- `Command::long_version`
- [clap_mangen](https://crates.io/crates/clap_mangen)for generating man page source (roff)
- [clap_complete](https://crates.io/crates/clap_complete)for shell completion support
- [clap-i18n-richformatter](https://crates.io/crates/clap-i18n-richformatter)for i18n support with- `clap::error::RichFormatter`

CLI Helpers

- [clio](https://crates.io/crates/clio)for reading/writing to files specified as arguments
- [clap-verbosity-flag](https://crates.io/crates/clap-verbosity-flag)
- [clap-cargo](https://crates.io/crates/clap-cargo)
- [colorchoice-clap](https://crates.io/crates/colorchoice-clap)

Testing

- `trycmd`
- `snapbox`
- `assert_cmd`- `assert_fs`

Documentation:

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [arg](https://docs.rs/macro.arg.html)
- Create an `Arg`
- [command](https://docs.rs/macro.command.html)- `cargo`
- Allows you to build the `Command`instance from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_authors.html)- authors - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the authors for the command from your Cargo.toml at
compile time in the form:
`"author1 lastname <author1@example.com>:author2 lastname <author2@example.com>"`
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_description.html)- description - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the description from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_name.html)- name - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the name from your Cargo.toml at compile time.
- [crate_](https://docs.rs/macro.crate_version.html)- version - `cargo`
- Allows you to pull the version from your Cargo.toml at compile time as
`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH_PKGVERSION_PRE`
- [value_](https://docs.rs/macro.value_parser.html)- parser
- Select a `ValueParser`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arg](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- The abstract representation of a command line argument. Used to set all the options and relationships that define a valid argument for the program.
- [ArgGroup](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgGroup.html)
- Specifies a logical group of [arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arg.html)
- [ArgMatches](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgMatches.html)
- Container for parse results.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- Build a command-line interface.
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- `Arg`- `ArgGroup`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ArgAction](https://docs.rs/enum.ArgAction.html)
- Behavior of arguments when they are encountered while parsing
- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)- Choice
- Represents the color preferences for program output
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValueHint.html)- Hint
- Provide shell with hint on how to complete an argument.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Args](https://docs.rs/trait.Args.html)
- Parse a set of arguments into a user-defined container.
- [Command](https://docs.rs/trait.CommandFactory.html)- Factory
- Create a `Command`
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromArgMatches.html)- ArgMatches
- Converts an instance of `ArgMatches`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- Parse command-line arguments into `Self`.
- [Subcommand](https://docs.rs/trait.Subcommand.html)
- Parse a sub-command into a user-defined enum.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/trait.ValueEnum.html)- Enum
- Parse arguments into enums.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2

## Expand description

`clap` is a simple-to-use, efficient, and full-featured library for parsing command line
arguments and subcommands when writing console/terminal applications.

`clap` is used to parse *and validate* the string of command line arguments provided by the user
at runtime. You provide the list of valid possibilities, and `clap` handles the rest. This means
you focus on your *applications* functionality, and less on the parsing and validating of
arguments.

`clap` also provides the traditional version and help switches (or flags) ‘for free’ meaning
automatically with no configuration. It does this by checking the list of valid possibilities you
supplied and adding only the ones you haven’t already defined. If you are using subcommands,
`clap` will also auto-generate a `help` subcommand for you in addition to the traditional flags.

Once `clap` parses the user provided string of arguments, it returns the matches along with any
applicable values. If the user made an error or typo, `clap` informs them of the mistake and
exits gracefully (or returns a `Result` type and allows you to perform any clean up prior to
exit). Because of this, you can make reasonable assumptions in your code about the validity of
the arguments.

The following examples show a quick example of some of the very basic functionality of `clap`.
For more advanced usage, such as requirements, conflicts, groups, multiple values and
occurrences see the [documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/), [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of
this repository or the [video tutorials](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLza5oFLQGTl2Z5T8g1pRkIynR3E0_pc7U).

**NOTE:** All of these examples are functionally the same, but show different styles in which to
use `clap`

The first example shows a method that allows more advanced configuration options (not shown in this small example), or even dynamically generating arguments when desired. The downside is it’s more verbose.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01b_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's full 'builder pattern' style of creating arguments which is
// more verbose, but allows easier editing, and at times more advanced options, or the possibility
// to generate arguments dynamically.
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("My Super Program")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("config")
                               .short("c")
                               .long("config")
                               .value_name("FILE")
                               .help("Sets a custom config file")
                               .takes_value(true))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("INPUT")
                               .help("Sets the input file to use")
                               .required(true)
                               .index(1))
                          .arg(Arg::with_name("v")
                               .short("v")
                               .multiple(true)
                               .help("Sets the level of verbosity"))
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg(Arg::with_name("debug")
                                          .short("d")
                                          .help("print debug information verbosely")))
                          .get_matches();
    // Gets a value for config if supplied by user, or defaults to "default.conf"
    let config = matches.value_of("config").unwrap_or("default.conf");
    println!("Value for config: {}", config);
    // Calling .unwrap() is safe here because "INPUT" is required (if "INPUT" wasn't
    // required we could have used an 'if let' to conditionally get the value)
    println!("Using input file: {}", matches.value_of("INPUT").unwrap());
    // Vary the output based on how many times the user used the "verbose" flag
    // (i.e. 'myprog -v -v -v' or 'myprog -vvv' vs 'myprog -v'
    match matches.occurrences_of("v") {
        0 => println!("No verbose info"),
        1 => println!("Some verbose info"),
        2 => println!("Tons of verbose info"),
        3 | _ => println!("Don't be crazy"),
    }
    // You can handle information about subcommands by requesting their matches by name
    // (as below), requesting just the name used, or both at the same time
    if let Some(matches) = matches.subcommand_matches("test") {
        if matches.is_present("debug") {
            println!("Printing debug info...");
        } else {
            println!("Printing normally...");
        }
    }
    // more program logic goes here...
}
```
The next example shows a far less verbose method, but sacrifices some of the advanced
configuration options (not shown in this small example). This method also takes a *very* minor
runtime penalty.

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/01a_quick_example.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's "usage strings" method of creating arguments
// which is less verbose
extern crate clap;
use clap::{Arg, App, SubCommand};
fn main() {
    let matches = App::new("myapp")
                          .version("1.0")
                          .author("Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
                          .about("Does awesome things")
                          .args_from_usage(
                              "-c, --config=[FILE] 'Sets a custom config file'
                              <INPUT>              'Sets the input file to use'
                              -v...                'Sets the level of verbosity'")
                          .subcommand(SubCommand::with_name("test")
                                      .about("controls testing features")
                                      .version("1.3")
                                      .author("Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
                                      .arg_from_usage("-d, --debug 'Print debug information'"))
                          .get_matches();
    // Same as previous example...
}
```
This third method shows how you can use a YAML file to build your CLI and keep your Rust source tidy or support multiple localized translations by having different YAML files for each localization.

First, create the `cli.yml` file to hold your CLI options, but it could be called anything we
like:

```
name: myapp
version: "1.0"
author: Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
about: Does awesome things
args:
    - config:
        short: c
        long: config
        value_name: FILE
        help: Sets a custom config file
        takes_value: true
    - INPUT:
        help: Sets the input file to use
        required: true
        index: 1
    - verbose:
        short: v
        multiple: true
        help: Sets the level of verbosity
subcommands:
    - test:
        about: controls testing features
        version: "1.3"
        author: Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>
        args:
            - debug:
                short: d
                help: print debug information
```
Since this feature requires additional dependencies that not everyone may want, it is *not*
compiled in by default and we need to enable a feature flag in Cargo.toml:

Simply change your `clap = "~2.27.0"` to `clap = {version = "~2.27.0", features = ["yaml"]}`.

At last we create our `main.rs` file just like we would have with the previous two examples:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// (Full example with detailed comments in examples/17_yaml.rs)
//
// This example demonstrates clap's building from YAML style of creating arguments which is far
// more clean, but takes a very small performance hit compared to the other two methods.
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
    // The YAML file is found relative to the current file, similar to how modules are found
    let yaml = load_yaml!("cli.yml");
    let matches = App::from_yaml(yaml).get_matches();
    // Same as previous examples...
}
```
Finally there is a macro version, which is like a hybrid approach offering the speed of the builder pattern (the first example), but without all the verbosity.

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate clap;
fn main() {
    let matches = clap_app!(myapp =>
        (version: "1.0")
        (author: "Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>")
        (about: "Does awesome things")
        (@arg CONFIG: -c --config +takes_value "Sets a custom config file")
        (@arg INPUT: +required "Sets the input file to use")
        (@arg debug: -d ... "Sets the level of debugging information")
        (@subcommand test =>
            (about: "controls testing features")
            (version: "1.3")
            (author: "Someone E. <someone_else@other.com>")
            (@arg verbose: -v --verbose "Print test information verbosely")
        )
    ).get_matches();
    // Same as before...
}
```
If you were to compile any of the above programs and run them with the flag `--help` or `-h` (or
`help` subcommand, since we defined `test` as a subcommand) the following would be output

```
$ myprog --help
My Super Program 1.0
Kevin K. <kbknapp@gmail.com>
Does awesome things
USAGE:
    MyApp [FLAGS] [OPTIONS] <INPUT> [SUBCOMMAND]
FLAGS:
    -h, --help       Prints this message
    -v               Sets the level of verbosity
    -V, --version    Prints version information
OPTIONS:
    -c, --config <FILE>    Sets a custom config file
ARGS:
    INPUT    The input file to use
SUBCOMMANDS:
    help    Prints this message
    test    Controls testing features
```
**NOTE:** You could also run `myapp test --help` to see similar output and options for the
`test` subcommand.

To try out the pre-built example, use the following steps:

- Clone the repository `$ git clone https://github.com/clap-rs/clap && cd clap-rs/tests`
- Compile the example `$ cargo build --release`
- Run the help info `$ ./target/release/claptests --help`
- Play with the arguments!

To test out `clap`’s default auto-generated help/version follow these steps:

- Create a new cargo project `$ cargo new fake --bin && cd fake`
- Add `clap`to your`Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
clap = "2"
```
- Add the following to your `src/main.rs`

```
extern crate clap;
use clap::App;
fn main() {
  App::new("fake").version("v1.0-beta").get_matches();
}
```
- Build your program `$ cargo build --release`
- Run with help or version `$ ./target/release/fake --help`or`$ ./target/release/fake --version`

For full usage, add `clap` as a dependency in your `Cargo.toml` (it is **highly** recommended to
use the `~major.minor.patch` style versions in your `Cargo.toml`, for more information see
[Compatibility Policy](https://docs.rs#compatibility-policy)) to use from crates.io:

```
[dependencies]
clap = "~2.27.0"
```
Or get the latest changes from the master branch at github:

```
[dependencies.clap]
git = "https://github.com/clap-rs/clap.git"
```
Add `extern crate clap;` to your crate root.

Define a list of valid arguments for your program (see the
[documentation](https://docs.rs/clap/) or [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory of this repo)

Then run `cargo build` or `cargo update && cargo build` for your project.

- `suggestions`: Turns on the- `Did you mean '--myoption'?`feature for when users make typos. (builds dependency- `strsim`)
- `color`: Turns on colored error messages. This feature only works on non-Windows OSs. (builds dependency- `ansi-term`and- `atty`)
- `wrap_help`: Wraps the help at the actual terminal width when available, instead of 120 characters. (builds dependency- `textwrap`with feature- `term_size`)

To disable these, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
```
You can also selectively enable only the features you’d like to include, by adding:

```
[dependencies.clap]
version = "~2.27.0"
default-features = false
# Cherry-pick the features you'd like to use
features = [ "suggestions", "color" ]
```
- **“yaml”**: Enables building CLIs from YAML documents. (builds dependency- `yaml-rust`)
- **“unstable”**: Enables unstable- `clap`features that may change from release to release

The following graphic depicts `clap`s dependency graph (generated using
[cargo-graph](https://github.com/kbknapp/cargo-graph)).

- **Dashed**Line: Optional dependency
- **Red**Color:- **NOT**included by default (must use cargo- `features`to enable)
- **Blue**Color: Dev dependency, only used while developing.

`clap`. You can either add it to the [examples/](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/v2.34.0/examples) directory, or file an issue and tell
